saints.name: Romanus the Melodist
saints.dates: Byzantine period; exact chronology not established here

summary.text: Romanus is remembered as a deacon and hymnographer associated with Constantinople. The OCA account describes his early difficulties as a singer, a traditional vision of the Mother of God, and his later hymn composition. It places his death around 556. The vision is presented as a feature of the received life, while particular hymn texts require their own identified editions.

blocks.text: GOARCH places Romanos in Emesa in Syria, probably in a Jewish family, and records Christian baptism and service as a deacon at Beirut. It links the Semitic idiom of his writings with that background. This biographical outline should be distinguished from the detailed story of his miraculous gift of song, transmitted in the later feast-day tradition.

blocks.text: The OCA narrative places Romanus at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Humiliated by unsuccessful reading during Nativity services, he receives a vision of the Mother of God and a scroll, then sings the Nativity kontakion. This is the transmitted hagiographic account of his gift.

blocks.text: Romanus (9), St., a celebrated hymn writer of the Eastern church, who is said to have written more than 1,000 hymns, of the kind called kontakia, a form which he probably invented. It perhaps derives its some what disputed name from the legend as to its origin, found in the Synaxasion of St. Romanus's day (Menaea, Oct. 1), which says that the Blessed Virgin appeared to him, and commanded him to eat a roll (kontakion) which she gave him, and that, obeying, he found himself endowed with the power of composing hymns. If he was the first who wrote kontakia, it is an argument in favour of placing him (as do Pitra and the Bollandists) in the reign of Anastasius I. (491-518) rather than of Anastasius II. (713-719). [H.A.W.]

GOARCH identifies the Nativity kontakion as a foremost example of his work and notes the influence of Ephraim’s hymns. The historical dictionary also distinguishes competing chronological placements, preferring the earlier Anastasius. Claims of a thousand compositions belong to the transmitted reputation; they should not imply that a thousand complete, securely attributed texts survive.
